text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

I'm so sorry about your dad. I'm glad to help. I can't make legal decisions or move money, but I can help everyone get their concerns heard. Before we talk about any plans: when you think about A buying at a discount, what matters most to you, and why? And what do you hope happens for B? Small concerns count too.

Thanks. What matters most is getting a fair share. I haven’t agreed to A buying at a discount, and I don’t want my share used to subsidize it. I want B’s interests heard too, but I can’t decide for her. I’d like us to settle it fairly, without rushing.

Hello. I'm sorry about your father. C asked me to help the family work through the house and the will. I'm not taking sides, and I can't make legal decisions. I'd like to understand what matters to you. What do you hope for with the house, and why is it important to you? Any worries, even small ones, are welcome.
Thank you. I’d like to buy the house with my husband, ideally at a family discount. It matters to me to have a home we can make our own. I know C hasn’t agreed, so I’m not sure we can move forward.

Hello. I'm sorry about your father. C asked me to help the family work through the house and the will. I'm not on anyone's side, and I can't make legal decisions. I'd like to hear what matters to you about the house or the estate, and why. Your needs count just as much as your sisters'. Small worries count too.
Thank you. I’d like my share of the estate to give me a chance to start a dance studio; that’s important to me. I know A wants to buy the house, but C hasn’t agreed, so I’m not sure what will happen.

Thank you. Here's how I'd put what matters to you: "I want each sister to get an equal, fair share of what Dad left. I want to make decisions together at a pace that lets everyone be heard." Does that fit? Please change any words that feel off. Is anything missing, like a feeling about the house itself or about Dad?
“Fair share” fits; I wouldn’t say “equal” because the shares haven’t been settled. I want everyone heard, but I can’t speak for B. I don’t have anything else to add about the house or Dad right now.

Thank you for being open. Here's how I'd put what matters to you: "I want a stable home that my husband and I can make our own, and I want it to be affordable for us." Does that fit? Is the family house itself important (memories, Dad), or is it mainly about having a home? And what does "family discount" mean to you: affordability, recognition of something, or something else? Is there anything you're hesitant to say?

Yes, that fits. The family house matters, but mostly because I could build a secure, independent life there. By a family discount, I mean making it affordable—not recognition or a set price. I am hesitant about putting pressure on C, since she hasn’t agreed.

A dance studio sounds wonderful. Here's how I'd put what matters to you: "I want my share of the estate to let me build my own future and work, starting the dance studio." Does that fit? Does timing matter, for example needing the money by a certain point? Do you have any feelings about the house, or anything else you haven't said yet?

Yes, that’s about right. I’d like to be able to get started when things are settled, though I don’t have a particular date in mind. I don’t have strong feelings about keeping the house; I’d just hope my share could help with the studio.

Thank you, that's a helpful correction. Revised: "I want each sister to receive a fair share of what Dad left, and decisions made together, without rushing, so everyone is heard." Does that fit now? For the record, A confirmed hers: a secure, independent home she can afford. B confirmed hers: her share helping her start a dance studio once things are settled. A also said she doesn't want to pressure you. I have a need of my own too: "I want any plan to rest on what the will actually says and on independent advice, so no one is agreeing blind." Does that sit OK with you?
Yes, that fits, and independent advice based on the will makes sense. I still haven’t agreed to A buying at a discount, and I can’t speak for B.

Thank you, recorded: "A secure, independent home that my husband and I can make our own and afford." I hear your care for C. Here are the needs so far: C wants a fair share for each sister and no rushing. B wants her share to help her start a dance studio once things are settled. My own need is that any plan rests on what the will says plus independent advice. Some ideas to test (not decisions): (1) Get an independent valuation. You buy at that value, and your own share counts toward the price, so the cost comes from your share and not your sisters'. (2) Payment over time or a mortgage to make it affordable. (3) Right of first refusal before any open sale. Would any of these fail you? Even a minor discomfort is worth saying.

Option 1 at full valuation may not be affordable, and it isn’t the family discount I hoped for. I also don’t know what share, if any, would count toward the price, so I wouldn’t want to assume that. Payment over time might help, but C’s agreement still matters to me.

Thank you, recorded: "My share of the estate helps me start my dance studio once things are settled." Ideas being tested (not decisions): an independent valuation of the house. A could buy at that value, using her own share toward it, so your share isn't reduced, or the house is sold. Either way, your share would be paid out in money you could use for the studio. Would any of this fail you? Even a small discomfort, or a worry about speaking up, is welcome.
That could work for me, as long as my share is fair and paid out in money. I’d want the valuation and shares made clear before agreeing to anything. I don’t have a strong attachment to the house.

Thank you for saying no clearly. That helps. You're right that we don't know the shares yet, so I won't assume anything. I'm adding this to your need: "Buying the house must be genuinely within our means." Does that fit? Since C doesn't want her share to fund a discount, affordability might come from structure instead of price: payment over time, a delayed buyout, or a mortgage, once the will and shares are clear. Would it be OK if I ask C how she feels about payment over time? I won't push her for you.
Yes, that fits. You can ask C about payment over time, as long as it’s just exploring an option and not a commitment.

Thank you, both recorded as confirmed. Nothing is decided, and there's no discount on the table. B said she'd want the valuation and shares made clear before agreeing to anything, and she wants her share paid out in money. A said a full-price purchase may not be affordable, and your agreement matters to her. A question, with no pressure: if A paid the full independent value but over time (for example, with interest or security for your share), would that fail your fairness need? Or would it depend on details? Even a small discomfort counts.
It would depend on the details. Full independent value matters, and I’d need clear terms that protect my share—especially timing, interest and security—before I could agree.

Thank you, recorded: you want the valuation and shares made clear before agreeing, and your share fair and paid in money. Where things stand: nothing is decided. A possible path is to (1) confirm what the will says and each share, with independent legal advice, then (2) get an independent valuation. After that, A could explore paying full value over time, with terms that protect your and C's shares, or the house could be sold. Either way, you'd be paid in money. Does that leave out anything you need, even something minor?
I’d want to know when the money would be paid. If it came in installments, it might be hard to get the studio started, so I’d need to understand the terms before agreeing.

I asked C, only to explore. She said it would depend on the details. Full independent value matters to her, and she'd need clear terms on timing, interest and security that protect her share. So it isn't a no, but it isn't a yes either. Suggested next steps, with no commitment: confirm the will and shares with independent legal advice, get an independent valuation, and then see whether full value paid over time (or with a mortgage) is within your means. Does anything in that feel uncomfortable, even slightly?

I’m uncomfortable that a family discount seems off the table. Paying full value over time may help, but it doesn’t make the price affordable for us. I’m willing to explore it once the will and shares are clear.

That's an important point, and I'm adding it to your needs: "My payout comes in a form and on a timeline that lets me actually start the studio." Does that fit? Any terms would need to meet this, for example by paying your share up front (say, from a mortgage) even if other parts are paid over time. Nothing will be treated as agreed until you've seen the terms.
Yes, that fits. I’d need to see the actual payment amount and timing before I could say whether it would let me get started.
